question: What is vendor-managed inventory?
html:
What vendor-managed inventory means

Vendor-managed inventory (VMI) means we manage a lab's stock of routine supplies for them. We track usage, set reorder points and restock before shelves run low. The customer no longer has to place each order. In our growth plan, VMI is one of the margin and retention levers alongside punchout ordering, private label and specialty verticals (Thomas Scientific growth plan).

How it works day to day

  • Agree the item list. We and the lab choose the consumables to cover, such as pipette tips, gloves, tubes and reagents.
  • Set stock levels. We agree minimum and maximum quantities for each item at each location.
  • Monitor usage. We track what the lab consumes through counts, scans or connected ordering systems.
  • Replenish automatically. We ship from our distribution centers when stock nears the minimum.
  • Review regularly. Stock levels change as the lab's work changes.

Why labs use it

  • Fewer stock-outs of critical consumables.
  • Less staff time spent counting and ordering.
  • Fewer rush orders and less excess stock on site.

Where it fits our plan

LeverRole in the plan
VMIMakes accounts sticky
Private labelHigher-margin mix
AI pricing toolsMargin uplift at large distributors
Punchout / digital orderingTable stakes for customers

Source: Thomas Scientific growth plan, generated Oct 6, 2026.

The plan targets named coverage of about 3,000 Pursue and Nurture sites by month 36. That is an est. assumption, not a forecast (Thomas Scientific growth plan). VMI is one way to hold those sites once we win them.

What we don't yet know

The context has no figures on current VMI accounts, VMI revenue, or retention rates for VMI versus non-VMI customers. These data would answer it:

  • Count of accounts on VMI today, and their share of revenue.
  • Retention and order frequency, VMI versus non-VMI.
  • Gross margin and cost-to-serve per VMI account.
  • Working capital tied up in consigned or on-site stock.

The last point matters most right now. The company is a stressed credit with a loan maturing in December 2027, and the plan puts cash ahead of growth (Thomas Scientific growth plan; Thomas Scientific public filings). Any VMI program that adds inventory to our balance sheet has to be tested against liquidity first.

Sticky, recurring accounts with predictable volume are part of the growth story that has to earn the refinancing, so VMI is worth building only where it raises retention without consuming cash we need for the loan.

Next actions

  1. Pull a baseline of current VMI accounts, revenue share and retention from the ERP and CRM.
  2. Estimate the working-capital cost per VMI account before expanding the offer.
  3. Pick a small set of Pursue sites for a cash-neutral VMI pilot tied to the inside-sales books.
  4. Report VMI retention and cash impact alongside the refinancing readiness metrics.

## How it works day to day

- **Monitor usage.** We track what the lab consumes through counts, scans or connected ordering systems.

- **Review regularly.** Stock levels change as the lab's work changes.

## Why labs use it

- Fewer stock-outs of critical consumables.
- Less staff time spent counting and ordering.
- Fewer rush orders and less excess stock on site.

## Where it fits our plan

| Lever | Role in the plan |
|---|---|
| VMI | Makes accounts sticky |
| Private label | Higher-margin mix |
| AI pricing tools | Margin uplift at large distributors |
| Punchout / digital ordering | Table stakes for customers |

The context has no figures on current VMI accounts, VMI revenue, or retention rates for VMI versus non-VMI customers. These data would answer it:

- Count of accounts on VMI today, and their share of revenue.
- Retention and order frequency, VMI versus non-VMI.
- Gross margin and cost-to-serve per VMI account.
- Working capital tied up in consigned or on-site stock.

The company is a stressed credit with a loan maturing in December 2027, and the plan puts cash ahead of growth (Thomas Scientific growth plan; Thomas Scientific public filings). 2. Estimate the working-capital cost per VMI account before expanding the offer.
3. Pick a small set of Pursue sites for a cash-neutral VMI pilot tied to the inside-sales books.
4. Report VMI retention and cash impact alongside the refinancing readiness metrics.
